To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
RAS blockade is recommended for all patients with diabetes and hypertension, but that the combination of a calcium-channel blocker with an ACE inhibitor may be the best option to achieve this goal.

the RAS blockade should be used for the prevention of cardiovascular disease in every patient with diabetes, and that the use of drugs other than ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers should be considered for the treatment of hypertension and prevention of cardiovascular disease, especially in type 2 diabetes.

the renin-angio-tensin system is involved in the development of diabetes and its complications; that RAS-active compounds are able to improve metabolic control in type 2 diabetes; and that RAS blockade is a cornerstone in preventing cardiovascular disease in diabetic patients, even if it is not always the most effective therapy.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following issues: 1) whether RAS inhibition should be recommended to every type 1 or 2 diabetic patient, and if so, which RAS-active compound should be preferred; 2) which antihypertensive drug is the best for treating hypertension in type 2 diabetics, either as a first-line treatment or as an additional drug to ACE inhibitors; 3) whether the use of RAS inhibitors and/or calcium-channel blockers should be extended to type 2 diabetic

the possible use of a new class of drugs in the treatment of diabetic patients with hypertension, namely, angiotensin II type 1 receptor antagonists, and with the role of RAS blockers as the cornerstone of the therapy of diabetic patients.
the role of the RDS in the development of hypertension and cardiovascular complications in type 1 and type 2 diabetic individuals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in the presence of hypertension and in patients at high cardiovascular risk (e.g., diabetic patients), RAS blockade is the best strategy to reduce cardiovascular events, whereas in patients with normal blood pressure, calcium-channel blockade may be a valid option, either alone or in combination with ACE inhibition.
the best treatment for hypertension and organ protection in diabetic patients is a combination of drugs with different mechanisms of action, including RAS blockers.

the best approach to the prevention and treatment of cardiovascular disease in patients with diabetes is to use the most effective antihypertensive drugs available, including RAS inhibitors, in combination with drugs acting on the calcium channels.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in the presence of hypertension, all type 2 diabetic subjects should be treated with a RAS inhibitor and that, in the absence of hypertension, all patients should receive a RAS inhibitor if they have microalbuminuria, retinopathy, or other signs of organ involvement, and should also receive a calcium-channel blocker if hypertension is present.
, in diabetic patients, a RAS blockade is the best strategy, but other drugs are also important for the treatment of hypertension.

, in type 2 diabetes mellitus patients, the RAS blockade with ACE inhibitors or angiotensin II receptor antagonists is the first choice in the treatment of hypertension and the prevention of cardiovascular events, but the addition of other antihypertensive agents, such as calcium-channel blockers, is often required.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, although RAS-active compounds are a cornerstone for treating hypertension in diabetic patients, the use of drugs other than those acting on the RAS may be useful in some cases, particularly when the RAS is not fully activated.
the RAS blockade is not the only way of preventing the development of micro- and macro-vascular complications in diabetic patients.

RAS blockade is not a panacea and that, in the presence of other antihypertensive agents, RAS inhibitors should be used only in patients with type 1 diabetes and in those with type 2 diabetes with microalbuminuria, overt nephropathy, and cardiovascular disease.
